facts.statement: Pterodaustro lived during the Early Cretaceous period, approximately 105 million years ago.
facts.quote: Its fossil remains dated back to the Early Cretaceous period, about 105 million years ago.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro is a genus of ctenochasmatid pterodactyloid pterosaur found in South America.
facts.quote: Pterodaustro (from Greek pteron, wing and Latin auster, south) is a genus of ctenochasmatid pterodactyloid pterosaur from South America.

facts.statement: The genus Pterodaustro was named in 1969 by José Bonaparte.
facts.quote: The genus was named in 1969 by José Bonaparte as an as yet undescribed nomen nudum.

facts.statement: The first valid description of the genus was published in 1970, with the type species Pterodaustro guiñazui.
facts.quote: The first description followed in 1970, making the name valid, the type species being Pterodaustro guiñazui.

facts.statement: Over 750 specimens of Pterodaustro have been collected from the Loma del Pterodaustro site, with 288 catalogued by 2008.
facts.quote: At the Argentine site, the just 50 m2 large "Loma del Pterodaustro", since then, during several expeditions, over 750 Pterodaustro specimens have been collected, 288 of them having been catalogued until 2008.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro is one of the best-known pterosaurs because fossils exist representing all growth stages, from egg to adult.
facts.quote: This makes the species one of the best known pterosaurs, with examples from all growth stages, from egg to adult.

facts.statement: Adult Pterodaustro reached a maximum wingspan of approximately 3 meters and a body mass of approximately 9.2 kilograms.
facts.quote: Pterodaustro had a maximum adult wingspan of approximately 3 m and a maximum body mass of approximately 9.2 kg.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro possessed a uniquely elongated tail with twenty-two caudal vertebrae, more than any other pterodactyloid.
facts.quote: Its tail is uniquely elongated for a pterodactyloid, containing twenty-two caudal vertebrae, whereas other members of this group have at most, sixteen.

facts.statement: The skull of Pterodaustro was very elongated, reaching up to 29 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: Pterodaustro has a very elongated skull, up to 29 cm long.

facts.statement: The modified teeth of Pterodaustro were arranged in two long grooves along the jaw edges rather than in separate sockets.
facts.quote: These teeth stand for the most part not in separate alveoli but in two long grooves parallel to the edges of the jaw.

facts.statement: The modified teeth of Pterodaustro were 3 centimeters long with a width of only 0.2 to 0.3 millimeters.
facts.quote: They have a length of 3 cm and are oval in cross-section, with a width of just 0.2 to 0.3 mm.

facts.statement: Research confirmed that the bristle-like structures in Pterodaustro's jaws were true teeth containing enamel, dentine, and pulp.
facts.quote: At first it was suspected these structures were not true teeth at all, but later research established they were built like normal teeth, including enamel, dentine and a pulp.

facts.statement: Despite being hard, the modified teeth of Pterodaustro could bend up to 45 degrees due to their extreme length-to-width ratio.
facts.quote: Despite being made of very hard material, they might still have been flexible to some extent due to their extreme length-width ratio, a bend of up to 45 degrees being possible.

facts.statement: The upper jaws of Pterodaustro carried very small teeth with a flat conical base and spatula-shaped crowns.
facts.quote: The upper jaws also carried teeth, but these were very small with a flat conical base and a spatula-formed crown.

facts.statement: The upper teeth of Pterodaustro were held by ligaments in a tooth pad covered with small bone plates rather than in sockets.
facts.quote: These teeth also do not have separate tooth sockets but were apparently held by ligaments in a special tooth pad, that was also covered with small ossicles, or bone plates.

facts.statement: Unlike most reptiles, the upper teeth of Pterodaustro were not replaced throughout its life.
facts.quote: It appears that they were not replaced, unlike the teeth of most other reptiles.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro likely used its tooth comb for filter feeding, a method similar to that of modern flamingos.
facts.quote: Pterodaustro probably strained food with its tooth comb, a method called "filter feeding", also practised by modern flamingos.

facts.statement: Gizzard stones have been found in the stomachs of Pterodaustro specimens, marking the first report of such structures in any pterosaur.
facts.quote: At least two specimens of Pterodaustro have been found, MIC V263 and MIC V243, with gizzard stones in the stomach cavity, the first ever reported for any pterosaur.

facts.statement: The abundance of small, hard-shelled aquatic crustaceans in the fossil site sediment supports the idea that Pterodaustro ate mainly these creatures.
facts.quote: Such invertebrates are abundant in the sediment of the fossil site.

facts.statement: Juvenile Pterodaustro grew rapidly in their first two years, reaching about half of adult size.
facts.quote: A study of the growth stages of Pterodaustro concluded that juveniles grew relatively fast in their first two years, attaining about half of the adult size.

facts.statement: Biomechanical modeling suggests Pterodaustro juveniles could fly, contradicting hypotheses that they could only glide early and fly late.
facts.quote: Biomechanical modelling suggests that Pterodaustro juveniles were capable of powered flight, contradicting the 'fly-late' and 'glide-early' hypotheses about changes in their flight capabilities over ontogenetic development.

facts.statement: A Pterodaustro embryo preserved in an egg was reported in 2004.
facts.quote: In 2004 a Pterodaustro embryo in an egg was reported, specimen MHIN-UNSL-GEO-V246.

facts.statement: Medullary bone tissue was reported in a Pterodaustro femur in 2009, potentially making it the first reported occurrence of such tissue in a non-dinosaurian reptile.
facts.quote: In 2009, possible medullary bone tissue was reported from the largest known femur of Pterodaustro (V 382). Medullary bone tissues are previously only known from modern birds that are laying eggs in reproduction, and some non-avian dinosaurs such as Tyrannosaurus rex, so this record would make it the first reported occurrence of a non-dinosaurian medullary bone.

facts.statement: In 2021, researchers suggested that the medullary bone tissue found in Pterodaustro might actually be crushed endosteal tissue.
facts.quote: In 2021, Padian and Woodward suggested that this tissue might instead represent a crushed endosteal tissue.

facts.statement: Comparisons of scleral rings suggest Pterodaustro may have been nocturnal, though this hypothesis has been questioned by some researchers.
facts.quote: Comparisons between the scleral rings of Pterodaustro and modern birds and reptiles suggest that it may have been nocturnal and similar in activity patterns to modern anseriform birds that feed at night, although the method of this research has been questioned by some researchers.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro likely required frantic, low-angled take-offs in open areas, similar to modern geese and swans.
facts.quote: Even with the pterosaurian quadrupedal launching mechanism, it would have required frantic and fairly-low angled take-offs possible only in open areas, much like modern geese and swans.

facts.statement: José Bonaparte initially assigned Pterodaustro to the family Pterodactylidae in 1970 and later to Pterodaustriidae in 1971.
facts.quote: Bonaparte in 1970 assigned Pterodaustro to the Pterodactylidae; in 1971 to a Pterodaustriidae.

facts.statement: Cladistic studies from 1996 placed Pterodaustro within the family Ctenochasmatidae alongside other filter feeders.
facts.quote: However, from 1996 cladistic studies by Alexander Kellner and David Unwin have shown a position within the family Ctenochasmatidae, together with other filter feeders.

facts.statement: A 2018 study placed Pterodaustro within the tribe Pterodaustrini of the family Ctenochasmatidae, in a basal position relative to Beipiaopterus and Gegepterus.
facts.quote: In 2018, a topology by Longrich, Martill and Andres recovered Pterodaustro within the family Ctenochasmatidae, more precisely within the tribe called Pterodaustrini, in a more basal position than Beipiaopterus and Gegepterus.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro adapted its beak with over 500 long and narrow teeth to filter food from water containing crustaceans and other small creatures.
facts.quote: Para aprovechar las grandes cantidades de crustáceos y otras pequeñas criaturas que viven suspendidas en el agua, el Pterodaustro adaptó su pico para filtrar su alimento con más de 500 largos y angostos dientes.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro had a long, narrow head, a curved beak, and a lower jaw with a thousand long, elastic bristles used to sweep the bottoms of shallow lagoons and seas.
facts.quote: Tenía una cabeza larga y estrecha, un pico curvado y una mandíbula inferior con un millar de cerdas largas y elásticas con las que "barría" los fondos de lagunas y mares poco profundos.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro had a wingspan of 132 centimeters, a head length of 23 centimeters, and a narrow head with a curved beak tip.
facts.quote: Pterodaustro tenía una envergadura de 132 cm; su cabeza medía 23 cm de longitud y era muy estrecha con un pico curvado en el extremo.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro is frequently nicknamed the "flamingo pterosaur" due to its diet potentially giving it a pink hue, similar to modern flamingos.
facts.quote: La dieta del animal podría haberle conferido una tonalidad rosada, otro probable rasgo en común con los flamencos de hoy en día; en efecto, Pterodaustro es frecuentemente apodado el "pterosaurio flamenco".

facts.statement: Pterodaustro was discovered in 1970 by paleontologists José Bonaparte and José Román Guiñazú in the Lagarcito Formation in San Luis, Argentina.
facts.quote: Fue descubierto en 1970 por los paleontólogos José Bonaparte y José Román Guiñazú en un paraje perteneciente a la Formación Lagarcito, en la región noroeste de la provincia de San Luis, en el centro de Argentina.

facts.statement: A site containing many fossils of this flying reptile was found in northern Chile by Kevin Pdian and Michael Bell.
facts.quote: Kevin Pdian, paleontólogo de la Universidad de California, junto a Michael Bell, hallaron un yacimiento con un gran número de fósiles de este reptil volador en el norte de Chile.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro was the first pterosaur found in the Southern Hemisphere.
facts.quote: Fue el primer pterosaurio hallado en el hemisferio sur.

facts.statement: Pterodaustro belongs to the parent group Lophocratia.
facts.quote: Parent group: Lophocratia

facts.statement: Pterodaustro is classified in the class Reptilia.
facts.quote: Class: Reptilia

facts.statement: Pterodaustro lived from the Aptian to the Albian stages, between 121.4 and 100.5 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Aptian to Albian (121.4 to 100.5 million years ago)

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that the formation containing Pterodaustro fossils originated from successive, sudden floods that destroyed the nests of this reptile.
facts.quote: Se sugiere que esta formación se originó cuando sucesivas y repentinas inundaciones arrasaron con nidales de este reptil.
